The framework reads the verse against Matt 16:18's *the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.* The gates-of-Sheol/Hades carry the power-of-death-and-the-grave that entered through the curse; the gates do not originate-with-the-Father; therefore the gates do not have permanence-against the assembly the King builds; therefore the resurrection-substance the King will demonstrate at the sign-of-Yonah breaks the gates' hold. The wisdom-stream had named the death-is-not-from-Yahuah substance; the King's-resurrection enacts the operative-substance.
new_note: *For Yahuah (God) made not death: neither has he pleasure in the destruction of the living.* (Wisdom of Solomon 1:13). *And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.* (Matthew 16:18). Wisdom of Solomon says it flatly: Yahuah (God) did not make death. It came in through the envy of the devil (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24) and through the sin in the garden; it is an intruder in his creation, not his design. That is why Yahusha (Jesus) can say the gates of hell, the gates of the grave, will not prevail against the assembly he builds. A thing the Father did not make has no permanent claim on what he did make. The grave's gates held every son of Adam until the one who said this walked out through them on the third day, and because he did, the gates will not hold his people either.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 1:13 — *Yahuah (God) made not death: neither has he pleasure in the destruction of the living.* Death is not of Yahuah's (God's) making, so the gates of the grave at Matthew 16:18 have no lasting claim on the assembly he builds.

apoc_text: For you have power of life and death: you leadest to the gates of hell, and bringest up again.
old_note: *For you have power of life and death: you leadest to the gates of hell, and bringest up again.* Wisdom of Solomon 16:13 names THE direct wisdom-stream verbal-anchor for the gates-of-hell-and-the-bringing-up-again substance. The framework reads the verse against Matt 16:18's *the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.* The wisdom-stream had named the architecture: the Father has-power-of-life-and-death; the Father leads-to-the-gates-of-hell-and-brings-up-again; the gates-of-Sheol/Hades do not have-final-authority-against-the-Father's-power-to-bring-up-again. The King's-promise that the gates-of-hell shall not prevail against the assembly enacts the wisdom-stream-substance at the gospel-pivot: the assembly built on the resurrected-King partakes-of-the-bringing-up-again the Father's-power has-always-held. The framework reads the substance in continuity with the resurrection-credential of the sign-of-Yonah pre-announced at v.4 and the explicit-third-day-raising at v.21.
new_note: *For you have power of life and death: you leadest to the gates of hell, and bringest up again.* (Wisdom of Solomon 16:13). *And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.* (Matthew 16:18). The gates of hell have no final say, because the one who leads down to those gates is the same one who brings up again. That is what stands behind the promise to Peter: the assembly is built on the King who would be raised the third day (he says so plainly at verse 21), and the gates that closed on him could not hold him, so they will not prevail against what he builds. The same chapter opens with the sign of Jonah (verse 4); the whole chapter is carrying this one truth, that the grave is a door the Father opens.
member_note: Wisdom of Solomon 16:13 — *you leadest to the gates of hell, and bringest up again.* The gates that could not hold the raised King will not prevail against his assembly (Matthew 16:18).

apoc_text: Did not the souls also of the righteous ask question of these things in their chambers, saying, How long shall I hope on this fashion? when comes the fruit of the floor of our reward?
old_note: *Did not the souls also of the righteous ask question of these things in their chambers, saying, How long shall I hope on this fashion? when comes the fruit of the floor of our reward?* 2 Esdras (4 Ezra) 4:35 names the wisdom-stream's articulation of the souls-of-the-righteous-in-their-chambers substance — the waiting-room of the righteous-dead between the first-coming and the resurrection. The framework reads the verse against Matt 16:18's gates-of-hell-shall-not-prevail substance. The chambers-of-the-righteous-souls are not the eternal-conscious-torment-hell of the inherited-Christian-doctrine; the chambers are the waiting-place-for-the-resurrection. The gates-of-Sheol the King names do not hold-the-righteous-souls-finally; the resurrection-architecture per Red Line #11's sequence the framework reads operates: the righteous-souls in-the-chambers await-the-first-resurrection at the King's-coming, when Sheol gives back-that-which-it-has-received (1 Enoch 51:1) and the chambers-deliver-those-souls-that-were-committed-unto-them (2 Esdras 7:32's parallel naming).
new_note: *Did not the souls also of the righteous ask question of these things in their chambers, saying, How long shall I hope on this fashion? when comes the fruit of the floor of our reward?* (2 Esdras 4:35). *And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.* (Matthew 16:18). The righteous dead are in chambers, Esdras is told, asking when the floor of their reward will come. They are not in torment and they are not in heaven; they are resting and waiting, and later in the book the chambers deliver up the souls committed to them at the resurrection (2 Esdras 7:32). That is what the King means when he says the gates of hell shall not prevail against his assembly. Sheol is a holding place with gates, and the gates do not hold his people past the day he calls them out. The chambers keep the righteous; they do not keep them forever.
member_note: 2 Esdras 4:35 — *the souls also of the righteous ask question of these things in their chambers.* The chambers hold the righteous until the resurrection; the gates of hell shall not prevail (Matthew 16:18).

apoc_text: As his mercy is great, so is his correction also: he judges a man according to his works
old_note: *As his mercy is great, so is his correction also: he judges a man according to his works.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 16:12 names the wisdom-stream's direct articulation of the Father-judges-a-man-according-to-his-works substance — both the mercy and the correction operating from the Father's-righteous-character. The framework reads the verse against Matt 16:27's *the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* The wisdom-stream had named the architecture of the judgment-according-to-works; the King's-second-coming-substance operates the same architecture at the eschatological-consummation. The framework reads this in continuity with the post-harvest-sifting per Red Line #11 — the works are the fruit-of-the-new-heart-that-internalized-or-did-not-internalize per the Yechezk'el (Ezekiel) 36:26-27 substance; the wisdom-stream had named the architecture; the King names the operative-form at the gospel-precision.
new_note: *As his mercy is great, so is his correction also: he judges a man according to his works* (Ecclesiasticus 16:12). *For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* (Matthew 16:27). Sirach holds mercy and correction in the same hand and says the measure of both is a man's works. Yahusha (Jesus) says the same about his own coming in his Father's glory: every man rewarded according to his works. Grace is the door home, not the cancelling of the reckoning. The judgment weighs the fruit, and the fruit comes from a heart that either received the new heart Ezekiel promised or did not.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 16:12 — *he judges a man according to his works.* Judged according to his works is the Son of Adam's reward at Matthew 16:27.

apoc_text: Make way for every work of mercy: for every man shall find according to his works.
old_note: *Make way for every work of mercy: for every man shall find according to his works.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 16:14 names the wisdom-stream's articulation of the every-man-shall-find-according-to-his-works substance. The framework reads the verse against Matt 16:27's reward-according-to-works at the Son-of-Adam's-coming. The framework reads this in continuity with the framework's-grace-and-the-opportunity-that-can-be-lost architecture — the grace is the door-home; the works are the fruit; the reward at the day-of-judgment operates according-to-the-fruit, in the post-harvest-sifting Matt 7:21-23 + Matt 13:36-43 + Matt 25:31-46 articulate at the gospel-substance the wisdom-stream had named.
new_note: *Make way for every work of mercy: for every man shall find according to his works.* (Ecclesiasticus 16:14). *For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* (Matthew 16:27). Sirach ties the two halves together: make way for every work of mercy, because every man shall find according to his works. Yahusha (Jesus) says the finding happens when the Son of Adam comes in his Father's glory. Mercy done now is what is found then. The door home is opened by grace; what is weighed at the judgment is what the one who came home did after he walked in.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 16:14 — *Make way for every work of mercy: for every man shall find according to his works.* Every man finds according to his works when the Son of Adam comes at Matthew 16:27.

apoc_text: Till he have rendered to every man according to his deeds, and to the works of men according to their devices; till he have judged the cause of his people, and made them to rejoice in his mercy.

The framework reads the verse against Matt 16:27's reward-according-to-works at the Son-of-Adam's-coming. The King's-articulation at v.27 carries-forward both halves: the reward-according-to-works for the sifted-wheat AND the judging-of-the-cause-of-the-Father's-people in the millennial-reign-on-the-earth. The framework reads this in continuity with the Tehillim (Psalm) 62:12 *thou renderest to every man according to his work* substance Romans 2:6 cites at the apostolic-level.
new_note: *Till he have rendered to every man according to his deeds, and to the works of men according to their devices; till he have judged the cause of his people, and made them to rejoice in his mercy.* (Ecclesiasticus 35:19). *For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* (Matthew 16:27). member_note: Ecclesiasticus 35:19 — *Till he have rendered to every man according to his deeds.* Reward according to works at the Son of Adam's coming (Matthew 16:27).

apoc_text: And the earth shall restore those that are asleep in her, and so shall the dust those that dwell in silence, and the secret places shall deliver those souls that were committed to them.

The framework reads the verse against Matt 16:27's Son-of-Adam-coming-and-rewarding substance. The resurrection-substance the wisdom-stream names at 2 Esdras 7:32 + 1 Enoch 51:1 + Wisdom of Solomon 16:13 precedes the rewarding-according-to-works at the day-of-judgment. The framework reads the sequence in continuity with the first-resurrection of Revelation 20:4-6 — the righteous-souls in-the-chambers (2 Esdras 4:35) are restored-and-delivered (2 Esdras 7:32) and the works-of-the-living-and-the-restored are sifted-and-rewarded (2 Esdras 7:35 + Sirach 16:12 + Matt 16:27).
new_note: *And the earth shall restore those that are asleep in her, and so shall the dust those that dwell in silence, and the secret places shall deliver those souls that were committed to them.* (2 Esdras 7:32). *For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* (Matthew 16:27). Ezra is shown the order: first the earth gives back those asleep in her and the secret places deliver the souls committed to them, then the Most High appears on the seat of judgment, and the work follows and the reward is shown (2 Esdras 7:33–35). Yahusha (Jesus) gives the same order in one sentence: the Son of Adam comes in his Father's glory, and then he rewards every man according to his works. Resurrection first, then the reward by works. The righteous who sleep are not being rewarded somewhere now; they rest in the places committed to them until the earth restores them, and the reckoning comes after.
member_note: 2 Esdras 7:32 — *the earth shall restore those that are asleep in her.* Resurrection first, then reward according to works, as the Son of Adam says at Matthew 16:27.

new_note: *And the work shall follow, and the reward shall be shewed, and the good deeds shall be of force, and wicked deeds shall bear no rule.* (2 Esdras 7:35). *For the Son of Adam shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.* (Matthew 16:27). member_note: 2 Esdras 7:35 — *the work shall follow, and the reward shall be shewed.* At Matthew 16:27 the Son of Adam rewards every man according to his works.

apoc_text: Admonish a friend, it may be he has not done it: and if he have done it, that he do it no more.
old_note: *Admonish a friend, it may be he has not done it: and if he have done it, that he may do it no more.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 19:13 names THE direct wisdom-stream verbal-anchor for the King's first-step assembly-discipline pattern at Matt 18:15. The framework reads the verse against *go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.* The wisdom-stream had named the direct-and-private admonition-of-the-friend substance at the wisdom-instruction-register; the King institutionalizes the same substance at the assembly's-procedural-register. The wisdom-stream-procedure and the King's-procedure cohere — confront-privately FIRST, with the substance aimed at restoration (*it may be he has not done it*; *he may do it no more*), not at public-shame or gossip. The substance reads in continuity with Vayikra (Leviticus) 19:17's *thou shalt in any wise rebuke thy neighbour.*
new_note: *Admonish a friend, it may be he has not done it: and if he have done it, that he do it no more.* (Ecclesiasticus 19:13). *Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.* (Matthew 18:15). Sirach's counsel is to go to the friend first, because he may not have done it at all, and if he has, so that he will do it no more. Yahusha (Jesus) makes that the first step when a brother trespasses: go to him alone, tell him his fault, and if he hears you the brother is gained. Both aim at restoration, not at shame or gossip — the private word comes before anything else, and the Torah had already told a man to rebuke his neighbour rather than carry a grudge against him in his heart.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 19:13 — *Admonish a friend, it may be he has not done it.* The private first step of Matthew 18:15 — go to him alone, and he may be gained.

apoc_text: Admonish your neighbour before you threaten him; and not being angry, give place to the law of the Most High.
old_note: *Admonish your neighbour before you threaten him; and not being angry, give place to the law of the Most High.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 19:17 names the wisdom-stream's articulation of the disposition-the-rebuker-walks-in at the assembly-discipline procedure. The framework reads the verse against Matt 18:15. The wisdom-stream names BOTH (a) the order — admonish BEFORE threatening, the substance of restoration before the substance of consequence — AND (b) the disposition — *not being angry, give place to the law of the Most High,* the wisdom-stream's articulation that the Torah-substance, not the rebuker's-own-anger, is the substance the rebuke-is-operating-from. The framework reads this in continuity with Galatians 6:1's *brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness* — the apostolic-restatement of the same disposition Sirach names the architecture for.
new_note: *Admonish your neighbour before you threaten him; and not being angry, give place to the law of the Most High.* (Ecclesiasticus 19:17). *Moreover if thy brother shall trespass against thee, go and tell him his fault between thee and him alone: if he shall hear thee, thou hast gained thy brother.* (Matthew 18:15). Sirach sets the order and the temper together: admonish before you threaten, and do it without anger, letting the law of the Most High govern the matter rather than your own heat. That is the spirit of the first step Yahusha (Jesus) gives — go to the brother alone and tell him his fault, which is admonition, not threat. The goal is to gain the brother, and a man cannot gain his brother while he is angry at him. The rebuke works when the Torah, not the rebuker's temper, is what it stands on.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 19:17 — *Admonish your neighbour before you threaten him.* The order and the temper of the private word in Matthew 18:15 — admonish first, and not in anger.

apoc_text: Admonish a friend: for many times it is a slander, and believe not every tale.
old_note: *Admonish a friend: for many times it is a slander, and believe not every tale.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 19:15 names the wisdom-stream's articulation of the two-or-three-witnesses substance the King institutionalizes at Matt 18:16. The framework reads the verse against *then take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.* The wisdom-stream names the substance the witness-verification-procedure protects against — slander, the false-tale, the unverified-charge. The King applies the Tanakh-Devarim (Deuteronomy) 19:15 evidentiary-standard the wisdom-stream had named the necessity-of at the wisdom-instruction-register. The substance protects both the brother-accused (from false-charge) and the brother-accusing (from inflated-or-fabricated charge); the witnesses serve as the substance-restraint on the offended-party as much as on the accused.
new_note: *Admonish a friend: for many times it is a slander, and believe not every tale.* (Ecclesiasticus 19:15). *But if he will not hear thee, then take with thee one or two more, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.* (Matthew 18:16). Sirach warns that many a report is slander and that not every tale should be believed — so go and admonish the friend rather than take the story as settled. Yahusha (Jesus) builds the same safeguard into the second step: if the brother will not hear, bring one or two more, so that every word is established in the mouth of two or three witnesses. The witnesses protect the accused from a false charge and the accuser from his own inflated one. What Sirach counseled as wisdom, the King set as procedure, and both rest on the Torah's rule that one witness is never enough.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 19:15 — *for many times it is a slander, and believe not every tale.* The two or three witnesses of Matthew 18:16 guard against the slander Sirach warns of.

apoc_text: It is much better to reprove, than to be angry secretly: and he that confesseth his fault shall be preserved from hurt.
old_note: *It is much better to reprove, than to be angry secretly: and he that confesseth his fault shall be preserved from hurt.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 20:2 names the wisdom-stream's articulation of the substance-of-the-open-reproof — the assembly-level-confrontation the King names at Matt 18:17's step-three (*tell it unto the assembly*) operates in the architecture-of-open-reproof the wisdom-stream had named the substance for. The framework reads the verse against the King's assembly-level-step. The wisdom-stream names the alternative-architecture: angry-secretly is the substance that does-not-restore; the open-reproof followed-by-the-brother's-confession is the substance that restores. The King's step-three is the assembly-level operationalization of the wisdom-stream's instruction; the assembly-as-a-whole carries the open-reproof-substance at the corporate-register the wisdom-stream had carried at the wisdom-instruction-register.
new_note: *It is much better to reprove, than to be angry secretly: and he that confesseth his fault shall be preserved from hurt.* (Ecclesiasticus 20:2). *And if he shall neglect to hear them, tell it unto the church: but if he neglect to hear the church, let him be unto thee as an heathen man and a publican.* (Matthew 18:17). Sirach says open reproof is far better than secret anger, and the man who confesses his fault when reproved is preserved from hurt. That is what the third step in Matthew is for: when the private word and the witnesses have both been refused, the matter is told to the assembly in the open, where it can still be confessed and the brother still preserved. Secret anger restores no one. Open reproof, met with confession, does — and only when even the assembly is refused does the brother put himself outside.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 20:2 — *It is much better to reprove, than to be angry secretly.* The open reproof before the assembly in Matthew 18:17 — the alternative to secret anger that restores no one.

apoc_text: Malice and wrath, even these are abominations; and the sinful man shall have them both.
old_note: *Malice and wrath, even these are abominations; and the sinful man shall have them both.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 27:30 names the wisdom-stream's articulation of the disposition-the-King-is-forming-against at Kefa (Peter)'s v.21 question. The framework reads the verse against Matt 18:21. The wisdom-stream had named malice and wrath as abominations-before-Yahuah at the wisdom-instruction-register; Kefa's *how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?* is the disciple-substance still-counting-the-offences, and the King's answer presses-past-the-counting into the disposition-of-no-malice. The framework reads this in continuity with the kingdom-citizens' fruits-of-the-Spirit substance (Galatians 5:22-23's love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness) the new-heart of Yechezk'el (Ezekiel) 36:26-27 forms-the-walker-into. FRAMEWORK-MAJOR.
new_note: *Malice and wrath, even these are abominations; and the sinful man shall have them both.* (Ecclesiasticus 27:30). *Then came Peter to him, and said, Adonai (Lord), how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times?* (Matthew 18:21). Sirach calls malice and wrath abominations, the portion of the sinful man. Peter comes to Yahusha (Jesus) still counting, asking how many times he has to forgive his brother, seven? A man who is counting offences is still holding them, and what he is holding is the malice Sirach names. The King's answer pushes past the count altogether, because the heart he is forming in his disciples is the new heart of Ezekiel 36:26, the one the Spirit moves to walk in the statutes, and that heart does not keep a tally against a brother.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 27:30 — *even these are abominations; and the sinful man shall have them both.* Malice and wrath as the sinful man's portion; Peter's *till seven times?* (Matthew 18:21) is still counting, and the King's answer leaves the count behind.

apoc_text: Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you, so shall your sins also be forgiven when you prayest.
old_note: *Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you, so shall your sins also be forgiven when you prayest.* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 28:2 names THE direct wisdom-stream verbal-anchor for the conditional-forgiveness-architecture the King names at Matt 18:21-22 and parable-extends at vv.23-35. The framework reads the verse against the King's *seventy times seven* answer + the unforgiving-servant parable + the chapter-closing *so likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not* (v.35). The wisdom-stream had named the substance directly: forgive-the-neighbour, and your-sins-shall-also-be-forgiven; the conditional-substance the King's parable extends into full narrative-form was already-articulated at the wisdom-stream-register. The framework reads this in continuity with Matt 6:14-15's Lord's-Prayer conditional-substance — *for if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.* The architecture-of-mercy-met-with-mercy runs the King's-teaching from the Sermon through the assembly-discourse; the wisdom-stream had named the substance the King operationalizes.
new_note: *Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you, so shall your sins also be forgiven when you prayest.* (Ecclesiasticus 28:2). *Yahusha (Jesus) saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.* (Matthew 18:22). Sirach says forgive your neighbour, and your own sins will be forgiven when you pray. Peter asks how many times, and Yahusha (Jesus) answers seventy times seven, then tells the parable of the servant who was forgiven a fortune and would not forgive a few pence, and closes it with the warning that the heavenly Father will do the same to anyone who does not forgive his brother from the heart. The Lord's Prayer had already made the same condition, forgive and be forgiven, forgive not and be not forgiven (Matthew 6:14–15). Sirach said it in one line; the King said it in a prayer, a number, and a story, and it is one teaching.
member_note: Ecclesiasticus 28:2 — *Forgive your neighbour the hurt that he has done to you.* The one line behind the King's *seventy times seven* (Matthew 18:22) and the parable that follows it: forgive, and be forgiven.

apoc_text: One man bears hatred against another, and does he seek pardon from Yahuah (God)?
old_note: *One man bears hatred against another, and does he seek pardon from Yahuah (God)?* Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 28:3 names THE direct wisdom-stream verbal-anchor for the unforgiving-servant's-grotesque-architecture the King names at Matt 18:33. The framework reads the verse against the lord's charge to the first-servant: *O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me: shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?* The wisdom-stream had named the grotesque-substance: one-man-bears-hatred-against-another and yet seeks-pardon-from-Yahuah for himself; the parable shows the same architecture in narrative-form — the first-servant has-been-forgiven and refuses-to-forgive. The lord's-wrath-and-revocation-of-the-forgiveness in the parable is the same architectural-substance Sirach had named the wisdom-instruction-substance-against. The kingdom-citizen's-substance must match the substance-received; the architecture is mercy-met-with-mercy at every register the wisdom-stream-and-the-King-and-the-apostles articulate.
new_note: *One man bears hatred against another, and does he seek pardon from Yahuah (God)?* (Ecclesiasticus 28:3). *Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee?* (Matthew 18:33). Sirach asks the plain question: a man holds hatred against another man, and he goes looking for pardon from Yahuah (God)? The parable in Matthew 18 puts that man in a story. He has just been forgiven everything he owed, and he takes his fellow servant by the throat over a trifle, and his lord asks him the very question Sirach asked, should you not have had compassion as I had pity on you? The pardon he had received was taken back. Mercy received has to become mercy given, or it does not stay.
